lesson.title: Letting Chance Sort the Volunteers
lesson.summary: Random assignment uses a chance mechanism to place experimental units into treatment groups, which balances known and unknown lurking variables so that any real difference in outcomes can be credited to the treatment itself.
lesson.body:
Random assignment is the process of using a chance mechanism, such as a shuffled deck of cards, a table of random digits, or a computer's random number generator, to decide which treatment each experimental unit receives. It is easy to confuse with random sampling, but the two ideas solve different problems. Random sampling decides who gets included in a study in the first place, so that the sample represents a larger population. Random assignment happens after the subjects are already chosen; it decides how those subjects are divided among the treatment groups inside an experiment.

The reason random assignment matters is that experiments work by comparing groups, and any comparison is only trustworthy if the groups were similar before the treatment was applied. Suppose researchers testing a new study technique let students choose which group to join. Motivated, organized students might gravitate toward the new technique, while less engaged students stick with the old one. If the new-technique group later scores higher, no one can say whether the technique caused the improvement or whether that group was simply stronger to begin with. This is exactly the kind of ambiguity that a lurking variable, in this case student motivation, introduces into the conclusion.

Consider a concrete case. A researcher has 30 volunteers for a study on whether a ten minute walk before a test improves scores on a memory quiz. She numbers the volunteers 01 through 30, then reads two digit groups from a table of random digits, skipping repeats and numbers above 30, until she has picked 15 people for the walking group; the remaining 15 become the no walk control group. Because the selection was governed entirely by chance rather than by who volunteered first or who looked more alert, neither group should be systematically different in age, fitness, sleep habits, or motivation before the walk happens. Any leftover difference between the groups is due to chance, and chance is something statisticians know how to measure and account for.

What makes this powerful is that random assignment tends to balance lurking variables the researcher has not even thought to measure, not just the ones on a checklist. It cannot guarantee that the two groups are perfectly identical, since chance can still deal one group slightly more strong sleepers or slightly more early risers. What it does guarantee is that any such imbalance is random rather than systematic, so it can be absorbed into the margin of error using the laws of probability rather than quietly biasing the results in one predictable direction every single time the experiment is run.

This is precisely why a properly randomized experiment, unlike an observational study, can support a cause and effect conclusion. In an experiment, the researcher actively imposes a treatment and controls who receives it through randomization; in an observational study, subjects arrive with their treatment already attached to them by their own choices or life circumstances. Random assignment is the single design feature most responsible for turning a mere association into a defensible claim about causation, which is why it sits at the foundation of every well designed experiment you will encounter in this course.
